questions.questionText: Which OSI model layer is responsible for logical addressing and routing packets between networks?

options.text: Layer 2 â€“ Data Link
Layer 3 â€“ Network
Layer 4 â€“ Transport
Layer 5 â€“ Session

explanation.correct: Layer 3 (Network) handles logical IP addressing and routing of packets between different networks. Routers operate at this layer.
explanation.incorrect: Layer 2 handles MAC addressing and local frame delivery. Layer 4 handles end-to-end transport. Layer 5 manages sessions.
explanation.examTip: OSI layers 1-7: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. Mnemonic: 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away'.

questions.questionText: What is the primary difference between TCP and UDP?

options.text: TCP is faster; UDP is slower
TCP provides reliable connection-oriented delivery; UDP is connectionless with no guaranteed delivery
UDP encrypts data; TCP does not
TCP is used for DNS; UDP is used for HTTP

explanation.correct: TCP establishes a connection via 3-way handshake, guarantees delivery, orders packets, and handles retransmission. UDP sends datagrams with no handshake, ordering, or retransmission.
explanation.incorrect: UDP is faster due to lower overhead. Neither encrypts by default. DNS uses UDP 53. HTTP uses TCP 80.
explanation.examTip: TCP = reliable (web, email, file transfer). UDP = fast (DNS, DHCP, VoIP, streaming, gaming).

questions.questionText: A host has the IP address 192.168.10.55 with a subnet mask of 255.255.255.0. What is the network address?

explanation.correct: With a /24 mask (255.255.255.0), the first three octets are the network portion. Network address = 192.168.10.0 (all host bits set to zero).
explanation.incorrect: 192.168.10.55 is the host address. 192.168.10.255 is the broadcast. 192.168.0.0 is a /16 network address.
explanation.examTip: Network address = IP AND subnet mask. Host bits all 0s = network. Host bits all 1s = broadcast.

questions.questionText: How many usable host addresses are available in a /28 subnet?

explanation.correct: A /28 has 4 host bits. Total = 2^4 = 16 addresses. Usable = 16 - 2 = 14 (subtract network and broadcast).
explanation.incorrect: 16 is total addresses. /27 gives 30 usable. /24 gives 254 usable.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an APIPA address that a host assigns itself when no DHCP server is reachable?

explanation.correct: APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) uses the 169.254.0.0/16 range. A host assigns itself an APIPA address when DHCP is unavailable, allowing local communication only.
explanation.incorrect: 192.168.x.x and 10.x.x.x are RFC 1918 private ranges. 172.16.x.x is also private. APIPA is specifically 169.254.x.x.
explanation.examTip: Seeing a 169.254.x.x address means the host can't reach a DHCP server. Check DHCP server, cable, and switch port.

questions.questionText: Which IPv6 address type is automatically configured on every IPv6 interface and is only valid for communication on the local link?

options.text: Global unicast (2000::/3)
Unique local (fc00::/7)
Link-local (fe80::/10)
Multicast (ff00::/8)

explanation.correct: Link-local addresses (fe80::/10) are automatically assigned to every IPv6 interface and are only usable within the local network segment â€” they are never routed.
explanation.incorrect: Global unicast = public IPv6 (routable). Unique local = private IPv6 (organisation-wide). Multicast = one-to-many delivery.
explanation.examTip: fe80:: = link-local (auto-assigned, non-routable). fd00:: = unique local (private). 2001:: = global unicast (public). ::1 = loopback.

questions.questionText: What protocol automatically assigns IP addresses, subnet masks, gateways, and DNS to network hosts?

options.text: DNS
DHCP
ARP
ICMP

explanation.correct: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) automatically provides complete IP configuration to hosts using the DORA process: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.
explanation.incorrect: DNS resolves names to IPs. ARP resolves IPs to MAC addresses. ICMP is for diagnostics (ping).
explanation.examTip: DHCP uses UDP ports 67 (server) and 68 (client). DORA: Discover (broadcast) â†’ Offer â†’ Request â†’ Acknowledge.

questions.questionText: Which DNS record type maps a hostname to an IPv4 address?

options.text: AAAA
MX
A
CNAME

explanation.correct: An A record maps a hostname to an IPv4 address (e.g., www.example.com â†’ 93.184.216.34).
explanation.incorrect: AAAA = IPv6 address. MX = mail server. CNAME = alias to another hostname.
explanation.examTip: DNS records: A(IPv4), AAAA(IPv6), CNAME(alias), MX(mail), NS(name server), PTR(reverse), SOA(zone authority), TXT(text/SPF/DKIM/DMARC).

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it correctly describes network protocols and ports.

explanation.correct: HTTP=TCP 80. SSH=TCP 22. HTTPS uses TCP 443 not UDP. DNS uses UDP 53 primarily but also TCP 53 for large responses and zone transfers.
explanation.incorrect: HTTPS is TCP only. DNS uses both UDP and TCP on 53.
explanation.examTip: Key ports to memorise: FTP(21), SSH(22), Telnet(23), SMTP(25), DNS(53), DHCP(67/68), HTTP(80), HTTPS(443), SMB(445), RDP(3389), SNMP(161/162).

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of NAT (Network Address Translation)?

options.text: To encrypt traffic between internal and external networks
To translate private IP addresses to a public IP for internet communication
To assign IP addresses automatically to hosts
To resolve hostnames to IP addresses

explanation.correct: NAT translates RFC 1918 private IP addresses to one or more public IPs, allowing multiple internal hosts to share a single public IP for internet access.
explanation.incorrect: Encryption = VPN/TLS. IP assignment = DHCP. Name resolution = DNS.
explanation.examTip: PAT (Port Address Translation) = many-to-one NAT using unique port numbers. Used by most home/office routers. Static NAT = one-to-one mapping.

questions.scenarioText: A network admin needs to divide the 192.168.1.0/24 network into 4 equal subnets.
questions.questionText: What subnet mask should be used?

explanation.correct: To create 4 subnets, borrow 2 bits (2^2=4). /24 + 2 = /26 (255.255.255.192). Each subnet has 62 usable hosts.
explanation.incorrect: /27=8 subnets, /25=2 subnets, /28=16 subnets.
explanation.examTip: Subnets needed â†’ bits borrowed: 2=1bit, 4=2bits, 8=3bits, 16=4bits. Add borrowed bits to prefix.

questions.questionText: Which protocol resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses on a local network segment?

options.text: RARP
ICMP
ARP
IGMP

explanation.correct: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) broadcasts a request asking 'who has IP x.x.x.x?' and the owner replies with its MAC address.
explanation.incorrect: RARP = MAC to IP (legacy, replaced by DHCP). ICMP = diagnostics. IGMP = multicast group membership.
explanation.examTip: ARP cache stores recent IP-to-MAC mappings. 'arp -a' shows the cache. ARP spoofing/poisoning is a Layer 2 attack.

questions.questionText: What is a default gateway?

options.text: The DNS server used by the host
The router interface that forwards traffic destined for other networks
The switch port a host is connected to
The DHCP server on the local subnet

explanation.correct: The default gateway is the router interface on the local subnet. Hosts send all traffic destined for remote networks to the default gateway for forwarding.
explanation.incorrect: DNS resolves names. The switch port is a physical connection. The DHCP server assigns IPs.
explanation.examTip: Default gateway must be in the same subnet as the host. If a host has no default gateway, it can only communicate locally.

questions.questionText: Match each protocol to its correct well-known port number.

explanation.correct: RDP=3389, SMTP=25 (secure submission=587/465), SNMP queries=161 (traps=162).
explanation.incorrect: SSH=22, Telnet=23, HTTPS=443, POP3=110, IMAP=143, Syslog=514, TFTP=69.
explanation.examTip: Full port list: FTP(20/21), SSH(22), Telnet(23), SMTP(25), DNS(53), HTTP(80), HTTPS(443), SMB(445), RDP(3389), SNMP(161/162).

questions.questionText: Which routing protocol is a link-state protocol that builds a complete topology map using Dijkstra's algorithm?

options.text: RIPv2
EIGRP
OSPF
BGP

explanation.correct: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is a link-state protocol that floods LSAs to all routers, building a complete topology map and using Dijkstra's SPF algorithm to compute best paths.
explanation.incorrect: RIP = distance-vector (hop count). EIGRP = Cisco hybrid. BGP = path-vector used between autonomous systems on the internet.
explanation.examTip: Link-state = OSPF, IS-IS. Distance-vector = RIP. OSPF metric = cost (inversely proportional to bandwidth).

questions.questionText: What is the function of BGP in internet routing?

options.text: To route packets within a single enterprise LAN
To exchange routing information between autonomous systems on the internet
To provide redundancy for the default gateway
To assign IP addresses to hosts automatically

explanation.correct: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the routing protocol of the internet, exchanging routing information between different autonomous systems (ISPs, large organisations).
explanation.incorrect: OSPF/EIGRP = interior routing within an AS. HSRP/VRRP = gateway redundancy. DHCP = IP assignment.
explanation.examTip: BGP = exterior gateway protocol (between ASes). OSPF/EIGRP = interior gateway protocols (within an AS). BGP uses TCP port 179.

questions.questionText: Which first-hop redundancy protocol is a Cisco-proprietary protocol that provides gateway redundancy?

options.text: VRRP
HSRP
GLBP
CARP

explanation.correct: HSRP (Hot Standby Router Protocol) is a Cisco-proprietary FHRP that provides a virtual IP gateway shared between an active and standby router, ensuring gateway availability if the active router fails.
explanation.incorrect: VRRP = open standard equivalent to HSRP. GLBP = Cisco's load-balancing FHRP. CARP = BSD/pfSense equivalent.
explanation.examTip: FHRPs: HSRP (Cisco), VRRP (open standard), GLBP (Cisco, load balancing). All provide a virtual gateway IP shared between multiple routers.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of QoS (Quality of Service) in a network?

options.text: To encrypt all network traffic
To prioritise specific types of traffic to ensure acceptable performance for time-sensitive applications
To increase the total available bandwidth on a link
To filter malicious traffic entering the network

explanation.correct: QoS marks, classifies, and prioritises traffic so time-sensitive applications (VoIP, video conferencing) get sufficient bandwidth and low latency even when the network is congested.
explanation.incorrect: QoS doesn't encrypt, increase physical bandwidth, or filter malware.
explanation.examTip: QoS for VoIP: mark voice traffic as DSCP EF (Expedited Forwarding). Guarantee bandwidth, limit jitter and latency. VoIP needs <150ms latency and <30ms jitter.

questions.questionText: Which network topology provides the highest fault tolerance by connecting every device to every other device?

options.text: Star topology
Bus topology
Ring topology
Full mesh topology

explanation.correct: A full mesh topology connects every node to every other node, providing maximum redundancy â€” multiple paths exist between any two nodes so a single link failure doesn't break connectivity.
explanation.incorrect: Star = central hub/switch (single point of failure). Bus = single shared cable (single point of failure). Ring = each node connected to two others.
explanation.examTip: Full mesh = n*(n-1)/2 links needed. Very expensive but maximum redundancy. Partial mesh = compromise between cost and redundancy.

questions.questionText: What type of address is ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff?

options.text: A multicast MAC address
A broadcast MAC address sent to all devices on the local segment
A loopback MAC address
An unassigned MAC address

explanation.correct: ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff is the Layer 2 broadcast address â€” all devices on the local network segment receive and process frames sent to this address.
explanation.incorrect: Multicast MAC addresses start with 01:00:5e (IPv4) or 33:33 (IPv6). No loopback MAC exists. Unassigned MACs are not ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff.
explanation.examTip: Layer 2 broadcast = ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff. Layer 3 broadcast = 255.255.255.255 or subnet broadcast. Both are confined to the local network/subnet.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between a public cloud, private cloud, and hybrid cloud?

options.text: Public = on-premises; Private = third-party; Hybrid = both
Public = shared infrastructure managed by provider; Private = dedicated for one org; Hybrid = combination of both
Private cloud means no internet connectivity
Public cloud is always more secure than private cloud

explanation.correct: Public cloud = shared multi-tenant infrastructure managed by a CSP (AWS, Azure, GCP). Private cloud = dedicated single-tenant, on-premises or hosted. Hybrid = combination with workloads spanning both.
explanation.incorrect: Cloud deployment is about tenancy and management, not just location. Private cloud can have internet access. Security depends on configuration.
explanation.examTip: Cloud models: Public (shared/CSP-managed), Private (dedicated/org-managed), Hybrid (both), Community (shared by similar orgs). IaaS/PaaS/SaaS are service models.

questions.questionText: What is a software-defined network (SDN)?

options.text: A network that uses only wireless connections
A network architecture that separates the control plane from the data plane, enabling centralised programmatic control
A virtual network created within a physical network using VLANs
A network managed entirely through command-line interfaces

explanation.correct: SDN separates the network control plane (decision-making) from the data plane (packet forwarding), allowing centralised software control of network behaviour through APIs.
explanation.incorrect: SDN isn't about wireless, VLANs only, or CLI management â€” it's about architectural separation and programmability.
explanation.examTip: SDN layers: Application (apps/APIs), Control (SDN controller), Infrastructure (switches/routers). Enables network automation and programmability.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a loopback address (127.0.0.1)?

options.text: To identify the default gateway
To test the local TCP/IP stack without sending traffic on the network
To identify all hosts on the local subnet
To represent an unassigned IP address

explanation.correct: The loopback address (127.0.0.1 or ::1 for IPv6) sends packets back to the local host's network stack, testing whether TCP/IP is installed and functioning correctly without physical network involvement.
explanation.incorrect: Default gateway = router interface address. Subnet broadcast identifies all hosts. Unassigned = 0.0.0.0.
explanation.examTip: ping 127.0.0.1 = test local TCP/IP stack. If this fails, reinstall network drivers. If this works but ping to gateway fails = physical/Layer 2 issue.

questions.questionText: A company has the network 172.16.0.0/16. An admin wants to create subnets that each support at least 500 hosts. What is the minimum prefix length they should use?

explanation.correct: /23 has 9 host bits: 2^9 - 2 = 510 usable hosts. This is the minimum prefix that supports 500+ hosts.
explanation.incorrect: /24 = 254 usable (too few). /22 = 1022 usable (more than needed). /25 = 126 usable (too few). /23 is the tightest fit.
explanation.examTip: Need hosts â†’ find host bits: >500 needs at least 9 bits (512-2=510). Prefix = 32-9 = /23.

questions.questionText: Which WAN technology uses labels to make forwarding decisions, allowing traffic engineering and QoS across service provider networks?

options.text: Frame Relay
MPLS
ATM
DSL

explanation.correct: MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) uses short labels rather than long IP lookups to forward packets, enabling traffic engineering, QoS, and VPN services across service provider networks.
explanation.incorrect: Frame Relay and ATM are legacy WAN technologies. DSL = broadband access technology.
explanation.examTip: MPLS is common in enterprise WAN services. Labels added at ingress LSR, switched by LSRs, removed at egress LSR. Enables Layer 3 VPNs for enterprises.

questions.questionText: What does CGNAT (Carrier-Grade NAT) do in the context of IPv4 address exhaustion?

options.text: It converts IPv6 addresses to IPv4 addresses
It allows multiple ISP customers to share a single public IP address using double NAT
It provides direct global IPv4 addresses to all end users
It encrypts all traffic between the customer and the ISP

explanation.correct: CGNAT (Large-Scale NAT) performs a second layer of NAT at the ISP level, allowing multiple subscribers to share the same public IPv4 address, extending the life of IPv4 addresses.
explanation.incorrect: CGNAT is not IPv4-to-IPv6 translation. It actually reduces the number of public IPs per customer. It doesn't encrypt traffic.
explanation.examTip: CGNAT means your 'public' IP is actually shared with many other customers. This can break some protocols (P2P, gaming, port forwarding). IPv6 deployment is the long-term solution.

questions.questionText: What does the acronym FQDN stand for and what is it used for?

options.text: Fully Qualified Domain Name â€” the complete hostname including all domain labels
Fast Queue Data Network â€” a QoS mechanism for prioritising traffic
Federated Query Distribution Node â€” a load balancing technique
Full Quality Distribution Network â€” a CDN architecture

explanation.correct: An FQDN (Fully Qualified Domain Name) is the complete domain name including all labels (e.g., mail.example.com.) â€” used to unambiguously identify a host on the internet.
explanation.incorrect: The other options are fictitious.
explanation.examTip: FQDN = hostname.domain.tld. (e.g., www.comptia.org). The trailing dot represents the DNS root. Used in certificates, DNS records, and service configurations.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of an SLA (Service Level Agreement) in networking?

options.text: To define technical configuration standards for network devices
To formally define expected performance levels, uptime guarantees, and remedies between a provider and customer
To document the network topology and IP addressing scheme
To outline the security policies applied to the network

explanation.correct: An SLA is a contract between a service provider and customer that defines measurable service metrics (uptime %, latency, packet loss, support response times) and remedies if targets are missed.
explanation.incorrect: Technical config = standards/procedures. Topology = network documentation. Security policies = security policy documents.
explanation.examTip: Common SLA metrics: uptime (99.9% = 8.7hrs downtime/year, 99.99% = 52min/year), MTTR (repair time), latency, packet loss, jitter.
